comment.value:
This paper proposes a novel AI-generated image detection algorithm based on the observation that real and fake images behave differently under DDIM inversion. Reviewers acknowledged the originality of this insight and appreciated the broad evaluation and strong empirical results.

In the initial reviews, several concerns were raised regarding the clarity and writing quality, efficiency limitations, lack of theoretical or rigorous explanation, evidence of design choices and dependencies, and incomplete coverage of related zero-shot methods and references. During the rebuttal and discussion, the authors clarified methodological details, added explanations, conducted additional ablations (e.g., different diffusion models, DDIM steps, CLIP vs. DINO features), and provided further quantitative results.

Most concerns were satisfactorily addressed, and the reviewers maintained positive ratings (three borderline accepts and one accept). Therefore, the paper is recommended for acceptance. The authors should ensure that the final version is revised to follow the suggestions from reviewers.

As the reviewer–author discussion phase has come to an end, we are delighted to have addressed most of the concerns, and no new questions have been raised. 

We greatly appreciate all reviewers for recognizing the contributions of our work, including the novelty and effectiveness of our method. At the same time, the reviewers have provided some insightful comments, such as on the computational efficiency of our method, additional ablation studies, and the clarity of the paper. We replied to the concerns of each reviewer individually and will incorporate the suggestions in the revised paper. 

We are grateful for the time and effort the reviewers have devoted, which will help improve the quality of this paper.

rebuttal.value:
>**Q1: Can you provide details on computational cost /complexity, and a comparison against other methods? Also provide details on compute resources (e.g. memory, inference time).**

**A1**: 
Thanks for your insightful review. Here, we primarily compare the computation cost with zero-shot methods, considering that most of them utilize diffusion models. To facilitate the comparison, we report the number of function evaluations (NFE) required to detect one image for each method. The detailed results are as follows:

|         | AEROBALDE | MIBD | ZeroFake | Ours-50steps | Ours-10steps |
|:-------:|:---------:|:----:|:--------:|:------------:|:------------:|
|  NFE    |    <1     |  8   |   1019   |      50      |      10      |
|  AP     |   73.5    | 73.9 |   65.5   |     97.5     |     97.1     |

AEROBLADE performs a single VAE reconstruction, which is less time-consuming than one diffusion model evaluation. MIBD by default uses 8 noise samples per image, while ZeroFake performs a full 999-step forward noising and a 20-step reverse denoising process. We also include the results of our method using a 10-step DDIM inversion, as we found it can achieve similar performance (refer to the Response 5).
In our tests, a single function evaluation using SD v1.5 on an A100 GPU takes approximately 0.14 seconds and consumes around 8.5 GB of memory.

Additionally, the computational cost of supervised methods is significantly lower than that of zero-shot methods, as most of them rely on lightweight network architectures. One exception is SIDA, which uses the large-scale multimodal model, LLaVA[8], for detection.

>**Q2:  Can you provide more theoretical analysis on why diffusion models predict their generated images more accurately?**

**A2**: Thanks for your valuable review. Although diffusion models are capable of generating realistic images, there still exist distributional differences between generated and real images[1,2]. Here, we provide further analysis from the perspective of score matching.

Diffusion models learn the gradient of the log-probability of the data distribution, known as the score function. This score indicates the direction from any given point toward the region of high data density. Generated images lie within the high density region learned by the model, while real images are located in lower density regions[3]. During the denoising process, the model's estimated scores tend to point toward the high-density region, i.e., the region where generated images reside. As a result, diffusion models make more accurate predictions for generated images.

>**Q3: Feature choice, one cna argue what is needed is only image-to-image similarity comparisons. Using CLIP is more expensive and perhaps unnecessary.**

**A3**: Thanks for your insightful review. Image-to-image comparison metrics such as MSE are highly sensitive to changes in the image. For example, altering the contrast of an image can result in a large MSE, even though the two images share the same semantic content. This pixel-level comparison is therefore not suitable for our method. Moreover, we observed similar settings in related works[3,4,5].

>**Q4: Can you compare CLIP features against alternative features such as DINO ?**

**A4**: Thanks for your constructive review. We conducted experiments by replacing CLIP with DINOv2, and the results are as follows (measured in AP):

|           | ForenSynths | GenImage | New Generator |  AVG  |
|:---------:|:-----------:|:--------:|:--------------:|:-----:|
|   CLIP    |    97.4     |  97.3    |     97.8       |  97.5  |
|  DINOv2   |    56.9     |  63.9    |     71.5       |  63.7  | 

As shown, the detection performance using DINO is significantly lower than that of CLIP. We speculate that this difference is mainly due to two reasons. First, unlike CLIP, DINO’s class token does not explicitly model global semantics using image captions. In addition, due to its self-supervised learning approach, DINO learns more robust representations. We observed that it is less sensitive to changes in image details. Meanwhile, we found that Rigid[4] also pointed out the significant impact of using CLIP versus DINO on detection performance.

>**Q5: Can you yield similar performance with fewer steps or by using only specific CLIP layers?**

**A5**: Thanks for your inspiring review. In our paper, we used 50-step DDIM inversion—a default setting—and simply averaged the similarity scores of class embeddings extracted from all layers of CLIP as the final metric. Here, we conduct experiments using fewer DDIM inversion steps and specific CLIP layers, and find that our method can achieve similar performance. The detailed results are as follows (measured in AP):

|           | ForenSynths | GenImage | New Generator |  AVG  |
|:---------:|:-----------:|:--------:|:--------------:|:-----:|
| 10-step   |    97.5     |  96.9    |     97.0       | 97.1  |
| 20-step   |    97.8     |  96.8    |     97.4       | 97.3  |
| 50-step   |    97.4     |  97.3    |     97.8       | 97.5  |

| layer1 | layer4 | layer7 | layer10 | layer13 | layer16 | layer19 | layer22 | layer24 |
|:------:|:------:|:------:|:-------:|:-------:|:-------:|:-------:|:-------:|:-------:|
|  57.8  |  62.3  |  86.3  |  92.9   |  97.8   |  97.6   |  92.8   |  85.4   |  82.4   |

Using only 10 DDIM inversion steps causes almost no degradation in our method's performance. Employing specific intermediate layers of CLIP can even bring slight improvements in detection performance(e.g., layer13). Moreover, the variation in detection performance across different layers is closely correlated with the curves presented in Fig4. These results are valuable, and we will include these results in the revised version to make our ablation study more complete.

>**Q6: The threshold selection for detection seems ad hoc and raises question about robustness and sensitivity to dataset. In Fig6, is the threshold 0.75 for a single dataset or multiple datasets?**

**A6**: Thanks for your review. The threshold 0.75 is applied across all datasets (line 264-266). 

>**Q7: In Fig3 the difference between real and AI-generated images on CycleGAN is less obvious as compared to diffusion models. Can you elaborate?**

**A7**: Thanks for your careful review. The real images in the CycleGAN dataset differ in resolution from those in the SD1.5 and Glide datasets, being 256x256 compared to the latter two, which are around 512 in both height and width. We speculate that this resolution difference may be the main source of the observed discrepancies. However, even under this condition, the real images in CycleGAN still pass through the nonlinear stage more slowly, which may explain why our method continues to achieve promising detection performance on this dataset.

**Q8: ProGAN is from 2018, have you tried training the supervised methods on more recent datasets? It would be interesting to see how they perform when trained on newer generation models rather than just older GAN data.**

**A8**: Thanks for your careful review. Training on ProGAN is a commonly adopted setting in related works[6,7]. According to your advice, we further trained NPR and UnivFD on the StyleGAN2 and SDv1.5 image datasets, respectively, considering they achieve the best performance among the two types of supervised methods. The experimental results (measured in AP) are as follows:

| Method              | ForenSynths | GenImage | New Generator |  AVG  |
|:-------------------:|:-----------:|:--------:|:--------------:|:-----:|
| NPR-StyleGAN2       |     90.0      |   73.0     |     73.5       | 78.8  |
| NPR-SDv1.5          |    77.7     |  88.7    |     92.6       | 86.1  |
| UnivFD-StyleGAN2    |    95.2     |  80.3    |     70.5       | 82.4  |
| UnivFD-SDv1.5       |    60.9     |  88.9    |     96.1       | 81.6  |

As shown, training on StyleGAN2 yields results similar to those obtained on ProGAN, with NPR even achieving lower detection performance. In addition, detectors trained on a specific generator tend to perform well under the cross-architecture setting, but they struggle to effectively detect images generated by cross-paradigm generators.


[1] Wang, et al. DIRE for Diffusion-Generated Image Detection. ICCV 2023

[2] Chu, et al. FIRE: Robust Detection of Diffusion-Generated Images via Frequency-Guided Reconstruction Error, CVPR 2025.

[3] Jonathan Brokman, et al. Manifold Induced Biases for Zero-shot and Few-shot Detection of Generated Images. ICLR 2025.

[4] He, et al. Rigid: A training-free and model-agnostic framework for robust ai-generated image detection. arXiv preprint arXiv:2405.20112, 2024.

[5] Sha, et al. Zerofake: Zero-shot detection of 445 fake images generated and edited by text-to-image generation models, CCS 2024.

**A1**: Thanks for your careful review. However, under these conditions, our method still achieves better average performance compared to other detectors (Fig. 5). >**Q1: Figure 3 should be better described. What is the meaning of this figure? How is the separation of the three stages determined?**

**A1**: Thanks for your valuable review. Figure 3 shows the L2 distance from each point, ${\hat{x}}_0(x_t)$, in the denoising trajectory to the straight line connecting the two endpoints, $x_0-{\hat{x}}_0(x_T)$. The linearity and non-linearity stage of the curve approximately reflect the three stages of the denoising trajectory. Since it is difficult to theoretically derive an exact threshold to segment these three stages, we manually performed a rough separation near the peak of the curve based on the curvature of each point.
Our goal is to use this figure to demonstrate the linear–nonlinear–linear structure of the denoising trajectory and show that fake images enter the second and third stages more quickly. This supports the hypothesis that the denoising outputs of generated images converge to original image faster. We will provide additional explanation for Figure 3 in the revised manuscript to enhance the clarity of our paper.

>**Q2: An ablation analysis using different diffusion models for the proposal should be included.**

**A2**: Thanks for your constructive review. In this paper, we conducted experiments using the SDv1.5 model. According your suggestion, we also evaluated our method with SDv2.1 and FLUX, considering their open-source availability and popularity. Note that although FLUX was proposed as a Flow Matching model, we still treat it as a diffusion model in this context. The experimental results are as follows (measured in AP):
| Diffusion Model | ForenSynths | GenImage | New Generator |  AVG  |
|:---------------:|:-----------:|:--------:|:--------------:|:-----:|
|     SDv1.5      |    97.4     |  97.3    |     97.8       | 97.5  |
|     SDv2.1      |    92.5     |  92.7    |     95.9       | 93.6  |
|      FLUX       |    84.8     |  88.3    |     81.9       | 85.3  |

SDv2.1 and FLUX achieve lower detection performance compared to SDv1.5, with the FLUX based detector performing the worst. We preliminarily speculate that this may be due to FLUX’s Transformer-based architecture, while most of the generators used in our experiments are CNN-based. The differences in induced bias between the two architectures may explain the performance gap. Nevertheless, FLUX based detector still achieve promising results. We will include these findings in the ablation study section of the revised version. Thank you again for your suggestion, which will make our work more complete.

Dear Reviewer kuMt, we thank you for recognizing the novelty of our work and for your careful review. We will first address the specific questions you raised, then provide a general response regarding the clarity issues.

>**Q1: It would have been more appropriate to include the more advanced gpt-image-1, which is currently the state-of-the-art for text-to-image generation**

**A1**: Thanks for your helpful review. As you mentioned, this API access was released close to the submission deadline. However, we have now conducted the experiment. We use the captions of real images from the New Generator as prompts and generate the corresponding fake images via API. The detection results are as follows (measured in AP):

| Method |  AP  | Acc  |
|:------:|:----:|:----:|
| Ours   | 99.9 | 98.2 |

We note that although GPT-generated images exhibit high visual quality, this does not necessarily make them more difficult to detect, which is consistent with findings from recent studies[7].

>**Q2: An ablation study on how the diffusion models affects results is also recommended.**

**A2**: Thanks for your valuable advice. In this paper, we conducted experiments using the SDv1.5 model. According your suggestion, we also evaluated our method with SDv2.1 and FLUX, considering their open-source availability and popularity. Note that although FLUX was proposed as a Flow Matching model, we still treat it as a diffusion model in this context. The experimental results are as follows (measured in AP):
| Diffusion Model | ForenSynths | GenImage | New Generator |  AVG  |
|:---------------:|:-----------:|:--------:|:--------------:|:-----:|
|     SDv1.5      |    97.4     |  97.3    |     97.8       | 97.5  |
|     SDv2.1      |    92.5     |  92.7    |     95.9       | 93.6  |
|      FLUX       |    84.8     |  88.3    |     81.9       | 85.3  |

SDv2.1 and FLUX achieve lower detection performance compared to SDv1.5, with the FLUX based detector performing the worst. We preliminarily speculate that this may be due to FLUX’s Transformer-based architecture, while most of the generators used in our experiments are CNN-based. The differences in induced bias between the two architectures may explain the performance gap. Nevertheless, FLUX based detector still achieve promising results. We will include these findings in the ablation study section of the revised version. Thank you again for your suggestion, which will make our work more complete.

>**Q3:  Section 2.2 omits all relevant zero-shot detection methods.**

**A3**: Thanks for your valuable review. First, we would like to clarify that we have provided sufficient introduction of the three zero-shot methods in the main text (lines 184–188) and Appendix A.1 (lines 511–516). We did not introduce zero-shot detection methods in Section 2.2 because the current mainstream detection approaches, i.e., high-frequency-based and semantic-based methods, cannot categorize them properly. Their underlying principles are also different from each other.
Moreover, we would like to emphasize that although other zero-shot methods also utilize diffusion models, our method is notably different from them. It is the first to leverage the intermediate denoising trajectory images in the diffusion process for detection. AEROBLADE[1] employs VAE reconstruction (line 511), while MIBD[2] computes similarity between the original image and noise (line 515). We believe there is a clear distinction between our method and the others, which is why we did not explicitly highlight this point in our paper.

>**Q4: Additional relevant work is missing, including ZED[3] and Rigid[4]. The authors are encouraged to include a direct comparison to ZED , and Rigid should be cited and briefly discussed for completeness.**

**A4**: Thanks for your careful review. We have cited ZED[3] in Sec 2.2 (line 90). However, to the best of our knowledge, ZED has not released its source code, which makes it difficult for us to reproduce their results. Although their paper includes detection results on some of the same generators, we note that their evaluation was conducted on the dataset they collected themselves, further preventing a direct comparison with our method. Regarding Rigid[4], we will cite it in the revised paper.

>**Q5: Low GLIDE Results for MIBD: The reported results for MIBD on GLIDE-generated images are not consistent with the original MIBD paper…**

**A5**: Thanks for your careful review. We are confident that we used the official MIBD source code and our experimental results are correct. Through careful check, we found that the inconsistent result arises from the fact that the Glide dataset used by MIBD is collected from the UniversalFakeDetect dataset[5], whereas the Glide images we used come from GenImage[6]. Furthermore, we noticed that the former used images generated with 100 and 50 sampling steps, while the latter used 1000 steps, resulting in higher-quality images. We suspect this is the main reason why our results on Glide differ from those reported in the original paper.

>**Q6: Most other zero-shot detection methods are relatively lightweight and efficient. In contrast, this method performs full DDIM inversion, which is both time- and resource-intensive...**

**A6**: Thanks for your insightful review. Here, we provide a brief analysis of the computational cost of our method and compare it with other zero-shot approaches. To facilitate the comparison, we report the number of function evaluations (NFE) required to detect one image for each method. The detailed results are as follows:

|         | AEROBALDE | MIBD | ZeroFake | Ours-50steps | Ours-10steps |
|:-------:|:---------:|:----:|:--------:|:------------:|:------------:|
|  NFE    |    <1     |  8   |   1019   |      50      |      10      |
|  AP     |   73.5    | 73.9 |   65.5   |     97.5     |     97.1     |

AEROBLADE performs a simple VAE reconstruction, which is less time-consuming than one diffusion model evaluation. MIBD by default uses 8 noise samples per image, while ZeroFake performs a full 999-step forward noising and a 20-step reverse denoising process(refer to Sec 4.3 of their paper). We also include the results of our method using a 10-step DDIM inversion, as we found it can achieve similar performance (refer to the Response 5 to the Reviewer RcDX). ZeroFake incurs significantly higher computational cost compared to other methods. Although our method requires more computation than AEROBLADE and MIBD, it brings over a 25% improvement in detection performance.

>**Q7: Regarding the issues of clarity and writing quality of our paper.**

**A7**: First, we apologize for any confusion caused by our oversight or typos that may have made our method description unclear. We perform DDIM inversion using SD v1.5. When computing the similarity, we calculate the average cosine similarities across steps and layers, and we acknowledge that the term $1/T$ was mistakenly omitted in Equation (5). Moreover, figure 6 indeed has the issue you pointed out, and Tables 1–3 provide the accurate results.
We will carefully revise and polish our paper to improve its clarity.
However, we sincerely ask you to consider the contributions of our work, which we believe outweigh these clarity issues.

summary.value: This paper proposes a novel zero-shot method for detecting AI-generated images by analyzing the convergence behavior of images under simulated DDIM inversion. The key insight is that generated images tend to converge more quickly toward a final image when passed through a reversed diffusion trajectory, compared to real images. The method is evaluated across a range of datasets, including both GAN and diffusion-based generators.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
1.	Original Insight: The observation that generated images converge faster than real images during simulated denoising is interesting and novel, despite being conceptually related to prior works.

2.	Breadth of Evaluation: The experimental setup is broad, spanning multiple generative models (GANs, diffusion, commercial models) and datasets. While DALLE 3 is used as a commercial model, it would have been more appropriate to include the more advanced gpt-image-1, which is currently the state-of-the-art for text-to-image generation. However, given that API access was released close to the submission deadline, the omission is understandable, but still worth noting. Additional robustness experiments are provided in the appendix, aligning with common expectations in this field.

Major Weaknesses:
1.	Clarity and Completeness of Method Description: The most significant issue is the poor and incomplete presentation of the core method. The actual computation of the proposed detection criterion is not formally described. For example, averaging cosine similarities across steps and layers is only briefly mentioned in the limitations section. Section 3.2 lacks formality, and the only equation provided suggests a sum (not average) over similarities without specifying how inner-layer representations are handled. Readers should not be required to inspect the code to understand the core algorithm. Additionally, important details like which diffusion model is used for DDIM inversion are missing. An ablation study on how the diffusion models affects results is also recommended.

2.	Section 2.2 omits all relevant zero-shot detection methods. AEROBLADE [47] and MIBD [7] are only discussed later in the paper and should be introduced in the related work section. This omission is critical, as both methods share some similar assumptions with this work and are conceptually aligned in meaningful ways.
a.	AEROBLADE also relies on the hypothesis that real and generated images interact differently with internal components of a diffusion model, which is conceptually similar to simulating the diffusion process as a behavioral signal.
b.	MIBD uses a combination of CLIP embeddings and a forward diffusion process in Stable Diffusion, closely paralleling this paper's use of CLIP embeddings and DDIM inversion. Both assume that generative origin can be inferred from differences in how images behave under diffusion-based transformations.
While the method is novel, these conceptual similarities are not acknowledged in Section 2 or elsewhere. Properly crediting related work would strengthen the paper’s framing and more clearly position its contribution within the existing literature.

3.	Furthermore, additional relevant work is completely missing: 
a.	ZED - D. Cozzolino et al ,  Zero-shot detection of ai-generated images, ECCV 2024.
b.	Rigid - Zhiyuan He et al. Rigid: A training-free and model-agnostic framework for robust ai-generated image detection. arXiv preprint arXiv:2405.20112, 2024.
The authors are encouraged to include a direct comparison to ZED (a), given its relevance as a recent zero-shot detection method published at ECCV 2024. While Rigid (b) is currently a preprint, it is still relevant and should be cited and briefly discussed for completeness.

4.	Writing Quality: The paper contains numerous grammatical and stylistic errors (e.g., line 74: starting a sentence with "And…", line 142: repeated words like "as as"). These issues appear throughout the paper and make it difficult to read and understand. While writing quality alone is not typically a reason for rejection, in this case it seriously impairs the communication of the core ideas. A substantial revision is needed to bring the writing to an acceptable standard for publication.

Minor Weaknesses:
1.	Terminology Consistency: The paper conflates synthetic images and deepfakes, which are well-differentiated in the literature. Clarifying this distinction would improve conceptual accuracy.

2.	Incorrect or Misleading Plots: Figure 6 appears to contain repeated plots for different generator-method combinations (e.g., ProGAN and StyleGAN for AEROBLADE and MIBD; Midjourney and DALL·E 2 for MIBD), even though Table 1 shows very different results for these cases. This suggests that the plots were either copied incorrectly or generated improperly. This reflects careless figure preparation and further contributes to the poor overall presentation of the paper.

3.	Low GLIDE Results for MIBD: The reported results for MIBD on GLIDE-generated images are not consistent with the original MIBD paper. This discrepancy raises concerns about either the evaluation setup or implementation and warrants rechecking. It is recommended that the authors verify this test to ensure correctness.

4.	Most other zero-shot detection methods are relatively lightweight and efficient. In contrast, this method performs full DDIM inversion, which is both time- and resource-intensive. An analysis of runtime and computational cost would help contextualize its practicality compared to existing approaches.

summary.value:
The authors propose a zero-shot method for synthetic image detection. The method is based on the observation that during the diffusion generation process, the synthetic images have a faster convergence than real ones. In particular, the proposed method reproduces the diffusion generation process of the image using DDIM inversion [53] and evaluates at each timestep the similarity between the original image and the denoised version comparing the features extracted from intermediate layers of CLIP.

The experimental section compares the performance of the proposal with respect to literature zero-shot methods [47,7,51] to detect images generated both by GANs and by Diffusion Models.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
- The main idea is clear. Moreover, the authors report all the details to reproduce the proposed technique.
 - The results show that the proposed method obtains SoTA performance also with post-processing operations.


Weaknesses:
- Figure 3 is not clear. What is the meaning of this figure? How is the separation of the three stages determined?
- The proposal adopts as diffusion model a Stable Diffusion V1.5 [48]. An analysis considering different diffusion models should be included.
- How does the proposal perform on other types of generative models, such as autoregressive models [A]?

[A] A. El-Nouby, et al. "Scalable pre-training of large autoregressive image models." arXiv preprint arXiv:2401.08541 (2024).

questions.value:
- Figure 3 should be better described.
- An ablation analysis using different diffusion models for the proposal should be included.
- Evaluating the proposal for detecting autoregressive models could be interesting.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths
The paper’s core contribution—leveraging denoising trajectory dynamics for zero-shot detection is noval. As a  zero-shot method, it eliminates the need for costly data collection and model training, making it scalable and accessible.

Weaknesses
1. The method’s performance degrades significantly under Gaussian blur or JPEG compression (Figure 5), with AP dropping to ~80% under these perturbations.
2. Key details for reproducibility are missing, such as hyperparameter tuning and exact prompts for "New Generator" images.

summary.value: This paper proposes a zero-shot method for detecting AI-generated images based on denoising trajectory analysis over time. The key idea is based on an observation that denoising outputs of AI-generated images converge to target images faster than those of real images. Based on this observation, the authors measure a similarity between the original image and intermediate outputs along the denoising trajectory as an indicator for image authenticity. The method focuses on the image generation process rather than by detecting any artifacts (artificialness) in an image. The method uses DDIM inversion to simulate the sampling process and uses CLIP to extract semantic features for computing similarity. Extensive evaluations are provided to show that this approach generalizes well across diverse generative models and datasets, outperforming both supervised and zero-shot detection methods.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:

1) Interesting observation and a novel idea (the speed of convergence), which is both easy to compute and yet effective. 
2) The method is training-free and applicable to different models.
3) Extensive validations.

Weakness:

1) Computational costs - compute CLIP features requires loading both CLIP and UNet at every diffusion time step, plus 50 DDIM steps - that's expensive compared to other methods. 
2) Limited theory - the convergence speed observation lacks stronger theoretical analysis beyond KDE. 
3) Feature choice - One can argue what is needed is only image-to-image similarity comparisons. Using CLIP (a Visual-Text cross-modality feature) is more expensive and perhaps unnecessary.  
4) Robustness - The threshold selection for detection seems ad hoc and raises question about robustness and sensitivity to dataset. In Fig6, is the threshold 0.75 for a single dataset or multiple datasets? If the threshold is sensitive to dataset distribution, that weakens the zero-shot claim.

questions.value:
1) Can you provide details on computational cost / complexity, and a comparison against other other methods? Also provide details on compute resources (e.g. memory, inference time).
2) Can you provide more theoretical analysis on why diffusion models predict their generated images more accurately?
3) Can you compare CLIP features against alternative features such as DINO [a]?
4) Running 50-step DDIM inversion plus extracting features from all CLIP layers seem expensive. Can you measure the actual computational overhead? Can you yield similar performance with fewer steps or by using only specific CLIP layers?
5) In Fig6, is the threshold 0.75 for a single dataset or multiple datasets?
6) In Fig3 the difference between real and AI-generated images on CycleGAN is less obvious as compared to diffusion models. Can you elaborate?
7) ProGAN is from 2018, have you tried training the supervised methods on more recent datasets? It would be interesting to see how they perform when trained on newer generation models rather than just older GAN data.

[a] Emerging properties in self-supervised vision transformers, ICCV 2021.

title.value: Denoising Trajectory Biases for Zero-Shot AI-Generated Image Detection

TLDR.value: A novel zero-shot generated image detection

abstract.value: The rapid advancement of generative models has led to the widespread emergence of highly realistic synthetic images, making the detection of AI-generated content increasingly critical. In particular, diffusion models have recently achieved unprecedented levels of visual fidelity, further raising concerns. While most existing approaches rely on supervised learning, zero-shot detection methods have attracted growing interest due to their ability to bypass data collection and maintenance. Nevertheless, the performance of current zero-shot methods remains limited. In this paper, we introduce a novel zero-shot AI-generated image detection method. Unlike previous works that primarily focus on identifying artifacts in the final generated images, our work explores features within the image generation process that can be leveraged for detection. Specifically, we simulate the image sampling process via diffusion-based inversion and observe that the denoising outputs of generated images converge to the target image more rapidly than those of real images.  Inspired by this observation, we compute the similarity between the original image and the outputs along the denoising trajectory, which is then used as an indicator of image authenticity.Since our method requires no training on any generated images, it avoids overfitting to specific generative models or dataset biases. Experiments across a wide range of generators demonstrate that our method achieves significant improvements over state-of-the-art supervised and zero-shot counterparts.
